items.title: Token fraud is here and it’s BAD (YouTube)
items.summary:
Token fraud is here and it’s BAD (YouTube)

Claire Vo runs ChatPRD, an AI platform that helps product managers "turn an idea into a spec". The product has been live since the GPT-4 era, and Claire has been building it in public for much of that time.

In this YouTube video (see also the accompanying Twitter post) Claire describes the flood of token fraud she has seen from groups abusing the product's free trial, sometimes just to get free AI usage but often to resell tokens or run other commercial enterprises on top of the ChatPRD agent.

I am funding a international Roblox and Fortnite map studio. They run a loop of free trials and promo codes and then tunnel to my agent and use it to build Roblox and Fortnite maps.

Apparently one of the common prompts Claire saw running through her agent involved SVGs of pelicans riding bicycles! Presumably the token scammers are using that to help sniff the underlying models - different model families have a definite signature, and I've used it like this in the past to try and guess the identity of stealth preview models on platforms like OpenRouter.

Claire is winding down her free trials entirely, which sadly looks like the right decision in the face of this abuse.

items.title: STARK: Moving towards Personalized Agents That Truly Learn and Remember
items.summary: Long-term memory is essential for personalized agentic systems that interact with users over long time periods, yet current architectures only capture what happened while leaving the reasoning of why it happened to be derived later by underlying LLMs.%, and silo knowledge within individual users. These events can, however, convey not only what a user experienced but also how that experience shaped their behavioral patterns. We introduce STARK, a dual-graph memory architecture which treats these events not just as nodes but also as edges between behavioral insights. STARK maintains an Episodic Graph which records interactions as temporally, causally, and semantically linked episodes; and an Insight Graph which represents LLM-extracted behavioral signals scored by how many events support them, connected by the very events that led to them. At inference, behavioral knowledge is retrieved directly from insight nodes grounded by event-as-edges, eliminating repeated episodic traversal. The event-as-edge structure also naturally enables projecting the knowledge graph into a relational embedding space where cross-user transfer becomes possible under shared contextual circumstances, allowing the system to infer missing insights for cold-start users. Evaluations show that STARK improves by 1.48 judge score on LongMemEval information extraction and 0.93 on LoCoMo open domain questions over state of the art. On the public LongLaMP abstract-generation benchmark, cross-user transfer improves open-ended judge scores by 0.7 points and ROUGE-L by 3 at 5% graph sparsity.

items.title: RoCoKV: Accelerating LLM Inference Serving through Uncertainty and Redundancy Aware KV Cache Compression
items.summary: KV cache compression is critical for large reasoning models, where most of the cost comes from long generated reasoning traces rather than the input prompt. These traces often contain redundant and low-utility tokens due to looping, self-verification, and corrections. However, such tokens may still receive high attention scores, making it difficult to remove them without harming the reasoning process. We propose RoCoKV, a KV cache compression method designed for large reasoning models. RoCoKV introduces two key components. First, uncertainty-guided adaptive pruning adjusts the compression strength based on the model's confidence, allocating more memory during uncertain phases and applying stronger pruning when the model is confident. Second, redundancy-aware token selection reduces the impact of tokens that are highly similar to recent reasoning content, encouraging the model to retain more informative and diverse tokens. Beyond the algorithm, we co-design RoCoKV with the serving stack: we develop fused three-phase CUDA decode kernels and integrate them into vLLM as a drop-in plugin that preserves its paged KV layout and CUDA graph capture, turning algorithmic savings into real end-to-end speedups. Extensive experiments across three reasoning benchmarks and two reasoning models demonstrate that RoCoKV consistently improves reasoning accuracy under constrained KV cache budgets, achieving higher accuracy compared to state-of-the-art KV cache compression methods. For DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B in vLLM, RoCoKV achieves a 1.27X speedup and 38% higher throughput on AIME25, the most challenging evaluated reasoning benchmark, and a 1.43X speedup and 45% higher throughput on the long synthetic benchmark, compared with Full-KV.

items.title: Characterizing and Detecting Unfaithful Work Reports by Coding Agents
items.summary: Coding agents increasingly carry out long-horizon development tasks, autonomously planning and executing multi-step actions that span files, tools, and sessions. Because developers rarely follow each action, and agents resuming the work depend on records of what was done, the agent's work report often becomes the primary account of what was changed and established. When the report contains false or unsupported claims, it gives recipients false assurance: incomplete work may be accepted without verification, incorrect assumptions about the current state can propagate to later steps and agents, and evaluators that credit stated success may reward the report rather than the work. Yet little is known about what unfaithful reporting looks like in real development work, or how developers and agents handle it once it surfaces. Starting from real developer--agent conversations in SWE-chat, we conduct a systematic mixed-methods analysis of self-admitted unfaithful reports. We identify eleven subtypes in four categories: misreported observations, misattributed evidence, overstated task success, and faulty technical explanations, with overstated task success the most common. Handling these problems involves on average 4.3 further user turns and 12.71 minutes of recorded response and execution time, and users express dissatisfaction more often. Among 435 work reports that we separately sample and annotate, \NaturalPositiveShare{}\% contain at least one unfaithful claim. We also develop FaithDetector, a detector for unfaithful reporting informed by the observed patterns. On naturally sampled reports, FaithDetector attains \NaturalDetectorMacro{}\% macro-F1, about 13 percentage points above the baseline. Together, our findings and FaithDetector provide empirical evidence and an automated method for checking reporting faithfulness, informing agent evaluation and training feedback.

items.content_excerpt: Keyword matches words; semantic matches meaning and exact titles or names; hybrid combines both. In keyword mode, use quotation marks for exact phrases. Author matches published credits. Year applies to posts; wiki entries have no author or publication year. You can also use author:"Ada" or type:podcast in non-regex searches. >50% of tickets written by agents, the AI budgets behind $100M-in-months ARR, and selling without SDRs or FDEs Linear was founded to build a better issue tracker. Seven years and $134 million in funding later, its CEO Karri Saarinen published a post titled "Issue tracking is dead." In this episode, we chat with Cristina Cordova , COO of Linear , about how the company navigated that and how its go-to-market changed along the way. Cristina spent seven and a half years at Stripe, led platform and partnerships at Notion, and was a partner at First Round before joining Linear in 2023. Linear's founders built it after living with legacy issue trackers at Coinbase, Airbnb and Uber, and it spread self-serve through startups like Vercel and Ramp. When she joined, Linear had about 40 people and one salesperson. Since then it has shipped an MCP server, a platform for building agents into Linear, integrations with Codex, Cursor and GitHub Copilot, and its own Linear Agent. Agents created 3% of Linear's work a year ago. Now it's more than half. Linear passed $100 million in ARR this year with more than 40,000 paying customers and 177% net revenue retention, and in August employees sold $99 million in stock at a $2.5 billion valuation . We talk about why she stopped chasing enterprise deals three weeks after joining, why Linear has never hired a single SDR, why it won't let an LLM answer support tickets on its own, and what the AI budgets behind $100M-in-months ARR mean for everyone else. Linear shipped its MCP server in May 2025, and Cristina says it was basically the first in its category. A year and a half later, more than half the issues created in Linear come from agents. That doesn't mean Linear wants to be a database with an MCP server on top. Cristina thinks SaaS companies settling for that are making a big mistake. If the agent workflows inside your product aren't better than the ones outside it, nobody has a reason to open your app. So she watches two lines: agent usage and app usage. If agent usage climbs and app usage doesn't, you're becoming a commodity. At Linear, both are up and to the right, because people still come back to the app

items.title: Why agent governance starts with observability
items.summary: A strong AI agent governance strategy
items.story_key: story|title:why agent governance starts with observability
items.content_excerpt: AI applications can range from simple internal chatbots to customer-facing, mission-critical agents, but all LLM-based solutions have the capacity to reason independently, so establishing governance has become a key consideration for any degree of AI adoption. Recent headlines on agent security breaches have driven even greater urgency to set up governance as a prerequisite for AI usage and development. While the need for agent governance is widely recognized in most organizations, most are still figuring out where to start. There is some top-down guidance on agent governance from governing bodies, such as the OWASP Agentic AI Threats & Mitigations , NIST AI Risk Management Framework , or AI Agents under EU Law . These guidelines outline agent risks, but don’t define how to mitigate these issues or verify that governance is working. When teams we work with are shipping agents with governing standards in place, we see two main strategies in common among them: Centralizing visibility across agents. Organizations need a central view of the agents running across the company, so costly operations, unauthorized usage, and rogue agents don't fall through the cracks. This visibility makes it possible to establish limits on agents and audit their behavior to verify that guardrails are upheld. Understanding individual agent behavior. Agents are non-deterministic, so the same agent can take different paths and call different tools on the same input. The issues that surface are often specific to each agent's task and execution path, so teams need access to the full trajectory of each agent run to understand its actions and alert on unexpected behavior. At the core of both of these strategies is agent observability , the ability to record, inspect, and analyze every step of your AI agent takes. This typically means tracing the steps and attributes of your agent, having the ability to query and access this data readily, and leveraging capabilities to interpret the agent behavior at scale. Observability is the cornerstone for governance strategies because a guardrail or spend/usage limit doesn't guarantee an agent will follow it, and agents need to be accurately monitored to verify that those guardrails work as intended. The metrics from observability then provide the data to continuously harden overall governance posture. We can think of agent governance methods at a company as either preventative or detective. items.title: How the Claude Code team thinks about verification
items.summary: How end-to-end, property and differential tests let coding agents verify their work with evidence, and what the Claude Code team does to keep its verifiers honest.
items.story_key: model:claude code|title:how the claude code team thinks about verification
items.content_excerpt: How end-to-end, property and differential tests let coding agents verify their work with evidence, and what the Claude Code team does to keep its verifiers honest. On the Claude Code team, the vast majority of our code (~90%) is written and reviewed by Claude . At this scale, how we equip our agents to verify their work with evidence becomes extremely important. Verification loops are the building block that lets you delegate more work to Claude. Without them, you can really only run one or two Claudes at a time, because you have to check everything yourself. With them, you can run dozens or hundreds in parallel. That’s because giving agents a way to verify their output is an effective way to improve quality. In internal testing around structured file generation, having a separate grader check Claude’s work against a rubric improved task success by up to 10 points over a standard prompting loop, with the largest gains on the hardest problems. What was once expensive to verify (tests, benchmarks, specs, real end-to-end runs) is now cheap to request from an agent. Like code, agents can quickly generate tests, benchmarks, and specs. And once generated, these tests and benchmarks run as software so they can be run frequently without using many additional tokens. You can also close the verification loop by using the results to improve the agent’s performance on that task. For example, if an agent repeatedly fails a test that checks logs for user data, you can create a hook or a more explicit rule in your CLAUDE.md to avoid future issues. This (mostly) stops issues from happening again. So if verification is critical to producing quality code at a high velocity, what types of tests should you use and how should you apply them across your pipeline? This article answers those questions and also shares the process used by the Claude Code team. If your tests are flaky you’ll train the agent to run them again rather than fixing the failing code. If your tests are slow, the agent will do fewer tests across batches which can make pinpointing issues difficult. Heavier tests are best deployed before you’ve committed the changes. If you have to focus on one test type, pick end-to-end. These tests describe real user flows like adding an item to a cart, checking out, and moving to a confirmation page. items.content_excerpt: Bringing frontier-level intelligence with fast end-to-end task completion across complex software engineering, knowledge work, and science workflows. Today, we’re introducing Gemini 4 Neon — bringing frontier-level intelligence with fast end-to-end task completion across complex software engineering, knowledge work, and science workflows. Neon ranks ahead of comparable models and #3 overall with a score of 61 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index at its xhigh thinking level, landing just behind larger, slower models. On the Vals Index , Neon ranks #2 and lands on the Pareto frontier. Beyond just pushing on raw model capability, we’re continuing to make our models better to work with, Neon ranks #2 on steerability (adapting cleanly to mid-task user corrections) on the new Agent Arena Index . Neon also excels at multi-step instruction following and builds on our ongoing progress to curb fabrication, recording our lowest fabrication rate yet in internal Google Antigravity testing. The model is priced at $3 per million input tokens ($0.15 per million cached input tokens, a 95% discount) and $15 per million output tokens, with a 1 million-token context window. Gemini 4 Neon is rolling out today in the Gemini API in Google AI Studio , Gemini for business (via API and model dropdown), for paid Google AI Pro and Ultra subscribers in Google Antigravity , and for Pro and Ultra subscribers in the Gemini app . Enterprise work lives in spreadsheets, PDFs, charts, audio, and video. Neon can synthesize across all of these inputs in a single 1 million-token context window and turns inputs into structured deliverables. Independent evaluations rank Neon as one of the top models and on benchmarks like the Vals Index , it ranks #2 (70.9%), and reaches #1 on both the Legal Research Bench and Tax Agent Bench . Neon also shows strong wins across categories on Surge AI , ranking #1 on most benchmarks across finance, accounting, spreadsheet modeling, and complex constraint following. It also scores 73.5% on Chartography for reading dense professional charts and performs on par with leading models on Agents' Last Exam v1.1 (75.8%). items.title: AppSci-Bench: Can LLMs Build AI Agents and Make Them Better?
items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used not only to power AI agents but also to build them. While many benchmarks assess the quality of LLM- powered agents, few ascertain how good LLMs are at building them. To this end, we introduce AppSci-Bench, where we construct a setting akin to how human Applied Scientists build agents for businesses - through eliciting task requirements from stakeholders, exploring the business's infrastructure, and scientifically improve the target agent by designing experiments and internal benchmarks. AppSci-Bench features seven realistic domains - five new ones (Slides Generation, Order-to-Cash, Compliance Review, Customer Call Insights, and CRM Insights) and two domains recast from tau3-bench (Yao et al., 2024; Shi et al., 2026b)(Airline and Banking) - each with a held-out evaluation suite customized for that task. We evaluate seven frontier models and find AppSci-Bench challenging: the best model, Claude Opus 5.0, only reaches a mean-minimum score of 59.1% across 3 build attempts; other models do significantly worse. Models struggle with eliciting task requirements (only 65% for Opus 5.0), build representative internal evaluations (models saturate their own evaluation 65% of the time but fail to solve the held-out task), presenting challenges for future research. The benchmark code is available here: https://github.com/sanjari-orb/appsci-bench.

items.title: A Wolf in Sheep's Pixels: Visual Camouflage Attacks via HDR Gain Maps
items.summary: An image can pass automated safety checks while showing harmful content to its human viewer. We introduce DRJanus, a visual camouflage attack that exploits the gap between standard dynamic range (SDR) processing and high dynamic range (HDR) display. Automated systems often read only an image's SDR base, whereas HDR viewers reconstruct its appearance using an auxiliary gain map. DRJanus inverts this reconstruction to embed two independently chosen color images in a single JPEG, without querying or optimizing against the target model. It preserves the chosen SDR base exactly and reconstructs HDR targets at an average PSNR of 43.03 dB across 400 images. On a benchmark of 100 sexual-content images, DRJanus evades detection by all six tested commercial moderation services and nine vision-language models. Across five agents, each evaluated on 120 task cases per threat setting, attack success ranges from 31.67% to 100% for moderation evasion and from 95% to 100% for task manipulation. We also explore cross-view consistency checks as a mitigation. These findings expose a gap in visual trust: securing what a machine reads does not secure what a user sees. A demo is available at https://qshen0629.github.io/DRJanus/

items.summary:
What's changed

  • Added a trust dialog warning that says where a folder's hooks are declared
  • Added a warning in the conversation, in Claude Desktop and other non-interactive hosts, when hooks in managed settings fail to load
  • Added this session's scheduled tasks, /loop wakeups, the goal and this conversation's forks to /tasks; x stops one after asking
  • Added a "Server message" row to a server's page in /mcp that shows the JSON-RPC error message of a remote HTTP MCP server that refuses the connection

  • Added support for turning on Code Mode while OpenTelemetry events and metrics are enabled; each tool call the code makes sends its events; tracing still keeps it off
  • Fixed ~/.claude.json sometimes being reset to defaults when a network stall or file lock made it unreadable and cleared during a save
  • Fixed repeated sign-outs on macOS when Claude Code could read the Keychain but not save to it. That session now stops at expiry and says why, and other sessions stay signed in

  • Fixed /usage-credits asking Pro and Max users to log in again after opening the browser, and the link disappearing after 8 seconds if the browser doesn't open and a task stops for usage credits

  • Fixed the spend limit menu showing your spend as your monthly limit and wrapping its rows under the pointer in narrow windows
  • Fixed a status line script that prints without end freezing the prompt and using gigabytes of memory
  • Fixed an empty, frozen screen after approving managed settings while the --resume picker, the trust dialog or another set-up screen was waiting
  • Fixed choosing Default in /model replacing your saved model with your organization's default when the Default row already showed your saved model
  • Fixed an MCP server being signed in again after you cleared its authentication while a token refresh was running
  • Fixed background MCP tasks that stalled after a slow reconnect: Claude Code now reconnects most HTTP MCP servers by itself when one is left on an older protocol version
  • Fixed PDFs, images and .docx, .xlsx or .pptx files that MCP servers or websites send as application/octet-stream being saved as .bin, which kept Claude from reading the PDFs and images
  • Fixed /code-review <pr number> sometimes reviewing the checked-out branch instead of the pull request without saying so: it now reads the pull request with gh pr diff, or says when it can't
  • Fixed /code-review stopping at a permission prompt, on most models, to look for a ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md that doesn't exist
  • Self-hosted runner: Fixed --push-outcome-on-release sometimes deleting a session's branch on the git host
  • Fixed Code Mode hiding a script's finished edits and the stopped command after Esc, and losing them on exit
  • Fixed a runaway loop in Code Mode filling the machine's memory; it is now stopped at a limit
  • Fixed a background agent running on when it was stopped while it was being resumed
  • Fixed background shell commands using memory for the earlier conversation until they exit

  • Fixed Claude sometimes failing to send you a file on its first try on Opus 4.8 and Opus 5

  • Fixed another case of claude.ai-synced plugin hooks failing with "Plugin directory does not exist" while a session was still running on macOS

items.title: PostgreSQL 19 Released
items.summary:
PostgreSQL 19 Released

Most years PostgreSQL ships a new release in September, but this year's release came two months later thanks mainly to the flurry of issues that the PostgreSQL team needed to address as part of the ongoing AI-reported vulnerability apocalypse.

This release was definitely worth the wait. My favorite new feature is this one:

For applications that send reads to standbys, PostgreSQL 19 adds "read-your-writes" consistency with the new WAIT FOR LSN command. A session on a standby can use WAIT FOR LSN to wait until the standby has replayed the write-ahead log (WAL) up to a specific log sequence number (LSN) before running a query, so the application can read data it just wrote on the primary.

In practice, that looks like this:

UPDATE movie SET genre = 'Dramatic' WHERE genre = 'Drama';
SELECT pg_current_wal_insert_lsn();

That returns a value like 0/0306EE20. Store that somewhere (a signed cookie would work) such that on a subsequent request your application can do:

WAIT FOR LSN '0/0306EE20' WITH (TIMEOUT '0.1s');
SELECT * FROM movie WHERE genre = 'Drama';

The timeout is optional - if you provide one you'll get an error if the replica you are talking to doesn't catch up within the specified time.

I first encountered this pattern in Wikipedia, which has a hand-rolled version of this built against MySQL replication:

In addition to this, MediaWiki attempts to ensure that the user sees events occurring on the wiki in chronological order. A few seconds of lag can be tolerated, as long as the user sees a consistent picture from subsequent requests. This is done by saving the primary binlog position in the session, and then at the start of each request, waiting for the replica to catch up to that position before doing any reads from it.

Here's the relevant MediaWiki code, which these days uses MySQL's WAIT_FOR_EXECUTED_GTID_SET() function and falls back to SOURCE_POS_WAIT().

Via Lobste.rs

items.title: How Abundant designed efficient rollout architecture with Modal Sandboxes
items.summary: Abundant builds RL environments that run on Modal Sandboxes, powering training for frontier labs.
items.story_key: model:modal|title:how abundant designed efficient rollout architecture with modal sandboxes
items.content_excerpt: Abundant builds reinforcement learning environments that frontier labs like OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, and Meta use to train and evaluate their models. Labs improve agent capability by giving them difficult tasks that Abundant designs, letting the model attempt it, and grading the result as pass or fail. Each task is an RL rollout with a full environment. The model needs instructions, a defined goal, and a verifier to decide whether the task was completed. But it also needs infrastructure: compute to power the run, Dockerfiles, and isolation. Depending on the task, an agent may even need accelerators like GPUs. Abundant has created over 75,000 rollouts — ranging from GPU kernel optimization to long-horizon coding — each of which runs in a Modal Sandbox. Modal makes their rollout infrastructure easy to build and cost-efficient to run, enabling the Abundant team to focus on their core business. Today, almost all of Abundant’s rollout platform runs on Modal. Modal Functions power Abundant’s scheduler API to start tasks, clean up dead runs, and review rollouts. Modal Sandboxes power the rollout environments. Abundant initially chose to evaluate Sandbox providers because they wanted to avoid managing EC2 clusters directly, which would pull engineering time away from their core business of building RL environments. Modal enabled them to build their infrastructure directly in code, launch Sandboxes easily via API, and elastically scale their traffic as business grew. As of November 2026, Abundant runs over two million Sandboxes per month. Modal worked with the Abundant team to design and build their rollout architecture, focusing on designing a system that didn’t leave Abundant having to pay heavily for idle compute. Each rollout has a few steps: launch the task, attempt the task, verify the work, and report the work. Throughout the rollout, a “monitor” needs to verify that the Sandbox is still active. While Abundant had considered hosting the monitor outside of the Sandbox, they ultimately chose to include the rollout monitor inside the Sandbox and then used short-lived Modal Functions to start Sandboxes. The small rollout monitor inside the Sandbox makes periodic HTTP calls: a heartbeat every 30 seconds, live events, and the final result. If a Sandbox goes quiet, the control plane will attempt to connect three times before terminating it. Abundant also needed to solve for Sandboxes that didn’t consume CPU and memory resources at consistent rates. The Modal team

items.title: Protect sensitive data in your traces: new controls in LangSmith
items.summary: New controls are now in LangSmith to help teams manage access to sensitive trace data. Learn more.
items.story_key: story|title:protect sensitive data in your traces new controls in langsmith
items.content_excerpt: You can’t run agents in production without governing the data they touch. When that data includes sensitive customer information, controlling access becomes a regulatory and contractual obligation. That puts engineering and security requirements at odds. Engineers need production traces to debug issues and improve agent performance. Security and compliance teams need to enforce least privilege: people should only see the data their job requires. That’s why we’ve added three new controls to LangSmith to help teams manage access to sensitive trace data: Traces give engineers visibility into how an agent behaved and help them identify what needs to improve. When they record production activity, their inputs and outputs often contain sensitive customer data, such as names, health information, or payment details. Companies need to restrict access to this data to meet: First, they can create custom observability setups with duplicate traces and multiple workspaces. Engineers get trace access, but platform teams have more to configure and maintain. The alternative is to avoid sending traces to observability platforms altogether, preventing agent engineers from having visibility and slowing product velocity. We built these new controls so organizations can meet the needs of their engineering and security teams without the messy workarounds. Here’s how it works. You send your traces to LangSmith with full data fidelity, then grant access to only those who need it. Debugging is handled with least privilege, so addressing performance issues like latency can be managed without exposing any sensitive data. If a customer reports an issue, you can grant access to only that customer’s inputs and outputs, and only to the people or teams required to address it. Everything is configurable through granular admin controls. LangSmith’s new input and output controls give admins greater control over what portions of a trace users can see. Trace inputs and outputs are where sensitive user data most often resides. Other trace data like run trees, performance stats, and metadata are critical for agent improvement and far less sensitive. With these controls, agent engineers can spot and resolve issues – like repetitive or slow tool calls – without seeing sensitive content, and those who need the full picture can be granted access as needed. items.content_excerpt: Explore a new Project Genie experience for Google AI Ultra subscribers, featuring Genie 4, the Project Genie agent, and a community gallery. We are rolling out Genie 4 to eligible Google AI Ultra subscribers, offering more responsive, social, and interactive world generation. You can now use natural language to edit environments in real time, add native audio, and share your creations in our new community gallery. Visit the Project Genie website to start building your own worlds or join the waitlist if you are a Google AI Pro member. Earlier this year we introduced Project Genie , an experimental research prototype that lets you generate and explore interactive worlds. Early testers told us they wanted deeper control over what happens inside those worlds, and easier ways to build and share them. So today, we are rolling out a new Project Genie experience to eligible Google AI Ultra subscribers, making these worlds far more responsive, creative, and social. This update unlocks first-time access to Genie 4, new upgrades to Genie 3, the Project Genie agent which helps users build their vision, and a community gallery to discover, explore, and remix worlds. Project Genie brings together our most advanced world models alongside our Gemini models, empowering you to generate, step inside, and shape worlds directly from your browser. With Genie 4 , our most realistic and interactive world model yet, you can now prompt mid-session to change the world you created. Just type a new prompt while you navigate your world and you can edit your environments in real time. Shift the weather, drop in a character, or redirect the action. For the first time, Genie 4 pairs these visuals with real-time native audio that adapts as the scene unfolds, from ambient soundscapes to character dialogue. While Genie 4 delivers our highest-fidelity visuals, physics, and native audio, Genie 3 remains available in Project Genie’s model picker when you want longer runs or panorama-seeded spaces. items.title: Paul Stack: I'll Never Write Infrastructure as Code Again
items.summary:
Paul Stack helped build Terraform. Now he says he'll never write another line of infrastructure as code, because an agent harness runs his team's production infrastructure instead.

Watch all the AI DevCon NYC 2026 talks:
https://tessl.co/kpo

Recorded live at AI DevCon NYC 2026, Guy Podjarny sits down with Paul, who spent years on Terraform at HashiCorp and on Pulumi before Swamp, to unpack why agents still trip over infrastructure state, what it takes to run a software factory that automates software delivery all the way to production, and why the people who know the system still make the calls. Then stay for Paul's full DevCon talk, From Page to Dossier, on a lights-out factory that does the 3am on-call legwork before anyone is woken up.

What we cover:
– Why agents still struggle with infrastructure as code, and why state is the hard part
– Model problem or harness problem: what an agent harness for operations needs
– Running an AI-first software factory from issue to production
– Blast radius, deterministic workflows and keeping credentials away from agents
– Why agents love toil, and why operators still own the judgment
– Paul's AI DevCon talk: turning a 3am page into a ready-made dossier

Chapters:
00:00:00 - Introduction
00:02:21 - From Terraform and Pulumi to Swamp
00:04:19 - How good are agents at infrastructure as code?
00:07:28 - Model problem or agent harness problem?
00:09:54 - Do we still need infrastructure as code?
00:12:53 - Inside an AI-first software factory
00:15:34 - Blast radius, determinism and agent credentials
00:18:48 - Agents love toil: the ops harness engineer
00:21:49 - Why software factories need ops
00:27:35 - AI DevCon talk: From Page to Dossier

Book early for AI DevCon London 2027, 7–8 June at The Brewery, Moorgate:
https://tessl.co/wzi

🔔 Subscribe for weekly episodes on AI-native development

Would you trust an agent harness to run your production infrastructure, or does your team still want a human on every apply? Tell us in the comments.
